problem.title: You landed here for one of four reasons.

cards.title: Your site takes four seconds to load.
cards.text: A visitor on a phone waits, gives up, and taps back to the search results. You paid to get that person to the page, and you lose them before your product appears.

cards.title: ChatGPT and Claude cannot see you.
cards.text: You ask an AI about your own category and it names three competitors. Your pages carry no structure a model can lift an answer from, so the model quotes someone who does.

cards.title: You vibe coded it, and it broke.
cards.text: The site went live in a weekend and looked fine at launch. Traffic grew, the content piled up, and the pages started to buckle under both.

cards.title: You have no site yet, and you need one.
cards.text: You are launching, or the current page is a form and a logo. You want a site built right the first time, fast on a phone and readable to an AI from day one, instead of one you pay to fix a year later.

faq.title: Answers before the first call.
faq.text: The questions teams ask most, answered without the sales detour.

items.q: Do you build websites from scratch?
items.a: Yes. If you have nothing yet, or a landing page holding the spot, I build the site from the ground up in Webflow or in code, and it ships fast on a phone and readable to an AI on day one. Most of my work is still sites that already exist and underperform, and that experience is what a new build gets you.

items.q: What PageSpeed score should my Web3 site have?
items.a: 90 or above on mobile. Most Web3 landing pages I audit score between 40 and 65. The causes repeat: uncompressed hero video, wallet connect scripts loading before anything renders, animation libraries pulled in on every page. All three get fixed without touching the design.

items.q: What is AEO and how does it differ from SEO?
items.a: SEO puts you in Google’s ranked list. AEO gets you quoted inside the answer that ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews write. The work overlaps, though AEO leans harder on structured data, semantic HTML, and content shaped so a model can lift a clean answer out of it.

items.q: Do you work in Webflow or custom code?
items.a: Both. I have built in Webflow since 2022, and I use Ship Studio with Claude Code where the project calls for code I own outright. The tool follows the project. Agencies that sell one stack will recommend that stack no matter what you need.

items.q: How do you choose between Webflow and custom code?
items.a: By who edits the site after launch. A marketing team shipping pages every week belongs in Webflow. A product team with engineers who own the repo belongs in custom code. Traffic, CMS depth, and budget move the answer around, but that one question settles most projects on the first call.

items.q: Will migrating my site hurt my rankings?
items.a: Not when the redirect map holds. Ranking drops after migration trace back to broken URLs, dropped metadata, and pages that vanish without a replacement. I map every existing URL before anything moves, keep the structure that earns traffic, and watch Search Console through the first month.

servicePages.painTitle: What a slow site actually costs you.

pain.title: You pay twice for every visitor.
pain.text: Ads and content bring someone to the page, then a four second paint sends them back to the search results. You paid for that click and got nothing for it.

pain.title: Google ranks the wait.
pain.text: Core Web Vitals are a ranking signal. A failing largest contentful paint holds a page down no matter how good the copy on it is.

pain.title: The desktop score is not the problem.
pain.text: A green number on a desktop test means little when your buyer is on a mid range Android over 4G. That is the device I test on.

works.title: The critical path
works.text: Render blocking scripts and stylesheets come out of the head, fonts get preloaded and metric matched, and the browser paints text on the first pass instead of the third.

works.title: The JavaScript you ship and never run
works.text: Most sites download a whole framework to animate three sections. I cut what is dead, defer what can wait, and load the rest only where it earns its bytes.

works.title: Media that holds the paint hostage
works.text: Hero images get sized, converted, and served at the width the layout actually asks for. Video that autoplays above the fold stops blocking the first frame.

works.title: Layout shift
works.text: Everything that arrives late gets its space reserved before it lands — images, embeds, and the font swap that quietly drops your headline one line down the page.

servicePages.proofText: The same tests, run before and after, with the raw reports attached. Median mobile PageSpeed across the last five projects is 97, up from 35, and largest contentful paint went from 4.1s to 1.2s on a throttled Moto G4.

faq.q: How fast can you make my site?
faq.a: Most sites I take on land above 90 on mobile. What I promise before the audit is the measurement, not a number: I profile the site first, tell you what each fix is worth, and you decide how far down the list to go.
No. Speed work is plumbing — the page looks the same and arrives sooner. Anything that would change a layout goes on a staging URL for you to review before it ships.
Yes. Webflow has its own ceiling and I know where it sits: what to cut, what to move out of the head, and the point where the platform itself is the bottleneck and a migration is the honest answer.
A typical pass runs one to two weeks from audit to shipped, depending on how much of the site is custom and how quickly your review comes back.

servicePages.ctaText: I run the audit and reply within a day with what I would fix first and what it is worth.

servicePages.metaTitle: Answer engine optimization (AEO) for Web3 and fintech | WaveWeb
servicePages.metaDescription: I structure your pages so ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews quote you by name instead of a competitor — and I measure it on the same prompts.
servicePages.subtitle: Ask a model about your own category and it lists three competitors. I structure your pages so the answer comes out of yours, with your name attached.
servicePages.painTitle: Why the answer names someone else.

pain.title: The click is disappearing.
pain.text: Your buyer asks a model instead of typing a query, reads the answer it gives, and never sees the ten blue links you optimised for.

pain.title: Models quote what they can parse.
pain.text: A page built out of nested divs and text baked into images gives a model nothing to lift. Structure, a clear question, and a direct answer give it a paragraph to quote.

pain.title: You cannot win a question you never answer.
pain.text: Most sites describe a product. An answer engine is looking for the sentence that answers the question your buyer actually asked, in the words they asked it.

works.title: Structured data that matches the page
works.text: Organization, Person, Service, FAQPage and breadcrumbs, wired into one entity graph so a crawler knows what the company is and who stands behind it, instead of nine disconnected blobs.

works.title: Answers written to be lifted
works.text: The question goes in a heading and the answer goes in the first two sentences under it. No preamble for a model to wade through before it reaches the part worth quoting.

works.title: Crawlable to the machines that matter
works.text: A robots.txt that lets GPTBot, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot in, a sitemap that stays current on its own, and content that renders in HTML rather than after a JavaScript bundle.

works.title: Entity signals off the page
works.text: The profiles, mentions and links that tell a search engine which company owns your name. Most AEO packages skip this part, and it is the part that decides whether you show up at all.

servicePages.proofTitle: How you tell whether it worked.
servicePages.proofText: I record the answers first: the same prompts, in the same models, before anything changes. After the work we run them again and you see where your name now appears and where it still does not. No agency dashboard, just the transcripts.

faq.q: What is AEO and how is it different from SEO?
faq.a: SEO earns a link in a list. AEO earns a sentence inside the answer. The work overlaps — both want a fast, crawlable, well structured page — but AEO optimises for being quoted rather than being clicked.

faq.q: Can you guarantee ChatGPT will mention me?
faq.a: No, and anyone who guarantees it is selling you something. Models change and none of them publishes a ranking. What I can do is remove every reason a model has to skip you, then measure the difference on the same prompts.

faq.q: Does AEO work hurt my Google rankings?
faq.a: The opposite. Structured data, fast pages and clear answers are what classic SEO has asked for all along. AEO is that same work, aimed at a reader that happens to be a model.

faq.q: How long before it shows up?
faq.a: Weeks, not days. Models refresh their view of the web on their own schedule, and a brand new domain waits longer than an established one.

servicePages.ctaTitle: Ask a model about your category.
servicePages.ctaText: Send me what it said and your URL. I reply within a day with why it named them and not you.

servicePages.metaTitle: Webflow migration: move your site into Webflow | WaveWeb
servicePages.metaDescription: I move your site into Webflow without losing a URL or a ranking, and hand your marketing team a CMS they can run without filing a ticket.
servicePages.titleStart: Your marketing team waits on an engineer
servicePages.subtitle: I move your site into Webflow, map every URL before anything changes, and hand your team a CMS they run themselves.

pain.title: Every change is a ticket.
pain.text: A price, a headline, a new case study — each one waits behind a developer queue. The site stops reflecting what you actually sell.

pain.title: Nobody wants to touch the theme.
pain.text: The site runs on a stack one person understood, and that person left. Updates feel risky, so nothing gets updated.

pain.title: A bad migration costs the traffic you already earned.
pain.text: Change the URLs without a map and the rankings you spent years building go with them. That is the part most migrations get wrong.

works.title: The URL map comes first
works.text: Before a single page is built I inventory every URL you have, match it to where it will land, and write the redirects. Nothing ships until that map is complete.

works.title: The design survives
works.text: You keep the site you paid for. I rebuild it in Webflow as a proper class system rather than a pile of one-off styles, so the next change is an edit instead of a rebuild.

works.title: Content becomes a Collection
works.text: Blog posts, case studies, job listings — whatever repeats becomes a CMS Collection your team fills through a form, with the template locked so nobody can break the layout.

works.title: It ships fast, not just finished
works.text: Webflow will happily serve a six megabyte page. The build goes out with the same speed work as everything else here: sized media, trimmed scripts, Core Web Vitals in the green.

servicePages.proofText: A staging URL you review before anything goes live, the full redirect map as a spreadsheet, a walkthrough of the CMS with your team on the call, and the speed reports before and after. Then the DNS switch, with me watching Search Console through the week that follows.

faq.a: Not when the redirects are right. Traffic usually dips for a week or two while Google re-crawls, then recovers. The damage happens when URLs change without a map, which is why the map is the first thing I build.

faq.q: Can you move my WordPress blog?
faq.a: Yes. Posts, categories, authors and images come across into CMS Collections, and the old URLs keep working through redirects.

faq.q: Will my team actually be able to run it?
faq.a: That is the point of the move. I lock the templates so an editor can change text and images without touching layout, and I walk your team through it before handover.

faq.q: How long does a migration take?
faq.a: Two to six weeks for most marketing sites, depending on page count and how much of the design has to be rebuilt rather than carried over.

servicePages.ctaTitle: Send me the site you want moved.
servicePages.ctaText: I reply within a day with the page count, the URLs that carry risk, and what the move would take.

servicePages.metaTitle: Migrate out of Webflow into code your team owns | WaveWeb
servicePages.metaDescription: You outgrew the platform. I rebuild your Webflow site as code in a repo your engineers own, keeping the design and every URL that earns traffic.
servicePages.subtitle: I rebuild your site as code your team owns, keep the design you paid for, keep the URLs that earn traffic, and hand your engineers a repository.

pain.title: The seat bill outgrew the site.
pain.text: You are paying per editor and per site for a platform you now use as a static host and little else.

pain.title: The thing you need next is not on the roadmap.
pain.text: A real search, a gated area, a pricing calculator that talks to your API. Every workaround is another embed, and every embed is more weight on the page.

pain.title: Your engineers cannot review a change.
pain.text: There is no diff, no branch, no pull request. Things go live because somebody clicked publish.

works.title: Same pixels, different engine
works.text: The rebuild matches the site you have — nothing gets redesigned unless you ask for it. What changes is everything underneath.

works.title: URL parity, checked line by line
works.text: Every live URL comes across at the same path, and I diff the two sitemaps before the switch. Anything that genuinely has to move gets a 301.

works.title: A repository your team recognises
works.text: Astro or Next depending on what your engineers already run, plain components, and no framework tax you did not ask for. It builds on Vercel or wherever you host today.

works.title: Content stays editable
works.text: Marketing does not lose the ability to publish. Copy lands in a CMS or in structured files, and we agree on that editing path before the first component is written.

servicePages.proofText: A Git repository with the full history, a build that runs on your own hosting, the redirect map, and the speed reports before and after. No part of the site needs me around to keep it running.

faq.a: No, unless you want it to. The default is a faithful rebuild: same design, same content, same URLs, new foundation underneath.

faq.q: What do you rebuild it in?
faq.a: Astro for a marketing site that is mostly content, Next.js when there is real application behaviour. If your engineers already run one of them, that settles it.

faq.q: Can marketing still publish without a developer?
faq.a: Yes, and it is a requirement rather than an extra. We agree on the editing path — a headless CMS or structured content files — before I write the first component.

faq.q: What happens to my Webflow CMS content?
faq.a: It comes with you. Collections export cleanly, and I map every field onto whatever replaces it.

servicePages.ctaText: I reply within a day with what the rebuild involves and where the platform is actually costing you.
